success.answerText:
The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open-source, open standard—originally created and released by Anthropic in November 2024—for connecting AI applications (like Claude or ChatGPT) to external systems such as data sources, tools, and workflows [3][4].

**Core idea:** Rather than building a custom, one-off integration for every data source or tool an AI system needs to use, developers can build against a single standardized protocol. Anthropic describes MCP as being like "a USB-C port for AI applications"—just as USB-C offers one standard connector for many devices, MCP offers one standard way to connect AI apps to external systems [3].

**Architecture:** MCP works through a client-server model. Developers can:
- Expose their own data/tools through **MCP servers**, or
- Build AI applications (**MCP clients**) that connect to those servers to access data and capabilities [4].

This enables secure, two-way connections between AI systems and things like local files, databases, content repositories, business tools (e.g., Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Postgres), and development environments [3][4].

**What it enables:**
- AI agents accessing personal tools like Google Calendar or Notion to act as more personalized assistants
- Coding assistants (e.g., Claude Code) generating apps directly from design tools like Figma
- Enterprise chatbots querying multiple internal databases via chat
- AI models controlling external hardware/software workflows, such as designing in Blender and sending output to a 3D printer [3]

**Why it matters:**
- **Developers** benefit from reduced complexity and development time when integrating AI with external systems.
- **AI applications/agents** gain access to a broad ecosystem of data sources and tools, enhancing capability.
- **End-users** get more capable assistants that can access their data and take actions on their behalf [3].

**Ecosystem:** MCP has since been adopted broadly—supported by AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT, and development tools including Visual Studio Code, Cursor, and others, allowing developers to "build once and integrate everywhere" [3]. Early adopters at launch included companies like Block and Apollo, along with dev-tool companies such as Zed, Replit, Codeium, and Sourcegraph [4]. MCP was created at Anthropic by David Soria Parra and Justin Spahr-Summers, and is maintained as a collaborative open-source project [4].
